checks_performed: Read only the authorized source JSON and draft JSON and independently compared the exact target with the draft’s final writeup and claims.
Reconstructed the normalization, quotient, parity, injection, canonical-member, incidence, averaging, and lattice proofs directly from the stated hypotheses.
Ran an exact-integer residual-case checker for the quantitative identities and the n=7, m=21 and m=23 arguments.
Exhaustively enumerated all labelled union-closed families for 1≤n≤5 using integer bit masks, with an independent all-assignment cross-check through n=4.
Checked the 19-member witness using integer bit masks: distinctness, all 361 ordered unions, minimum positive size, and every element frequency.

claims.claim: A hypothetical counterexample may be assumed to contain the empty set and to have ground set equal to the union of its members.
claims.evidence: Let U be the union of the finitely many members. Repeated union closure gives U∈F, and deleting X\U removes only zero-frequency elements. If ∅ is absent, adjoining it preserves union closure and all frequencies. A strict violation d_x<m/2 remains strict because d_x<m/2<(m+1)/2.
claims.search_method: Direct finite-set normalization proof, including preservation of the strict counterexample inequalities.

claims.claim: Equivalent active elements can be identified without changing the number of members or any relevant frequency.
claims.evidence: Equal incidence columns make every member a union of equivalence classes. Projection to one representative per active class commutes with unions and preserves class frequencies. It is injective because two distinct members differ on an entire class, so the family cardinality is unchanged and the projected active columns are pairwise distinct.
claims.search_method: Direct verification of the incidence-equivalence quotient and its injectivity.

claims.claim: If any counterexample exists, then a counterexample containing ∅ and having odd cardinality exists.
claims.evidence: After adjoining ∅, an odd-sized counterexample is already suitable. If its size is 2k, remove a minimum-cardinality nonempty member S. If retained A,B had A∪B=S, any nonempty one would be a subset of S with size at least |S| and hence would equal the removed S, so closure is preserved. Frequencies remain at most k−1<(2k−1)/2. A counterexample cannot have only ∅ and one nonempty member, so a nonempty member remains.
claims.search_method: Direct parity-reduction proof with all closure and nontriviality cases checked.

claims.claim: A union-closed family containing a singleton satisfies Frankl’s bound.
claims.evidence: For {x}∈F, the map A↦A∪{x} sends every member avoiding x to a member containing x. Deleting x recovers A, so the map is injective. Consequently at least half the members contain x.

claims.claim: A union-closed family containing a two-element member satisfies Frankl’s bound.
claims.evidence: For {x,y}∈F, partition the family into neither/only-x/only-y/both cells N,X,Y,B. Union with {x,y} injects N into B. Hence d_x+d_y=|F|+|B|−|N|≥|F|, so at least one frequency is at least |F|/2.
claims.search_method: Direct four-cell counting and injection proof.

claims.claim: Every separating union-closed family on n active elements has an element of frequency at least n; hence it satisfies Frankl’s bound whenever |F|≤2n.
claims.evidence: Order d_1≤⋯≤d_n. For i<j, separation and the frequency order imply that some member contains x_j but not x_i. Thus M_i, the union of all members avoiding x_i, exists, avoids x_i, and contains x_{i+1},…,x_n. For i<j, M_i contains x_j while M_j does not, so M_1,…,M_{n−1} are distinct. Together with X they give n distinct members containing x_n. Therefore d_n≥n, which is at least |F|/2 when |F|≤2n.
claims.search_method: Direct reconstruction of the canonical-union argument, including the distinctness step.

claims.claim: For a separating family containing ∅, an exact incidence lower bound is available.
claims.evidence: The distinct canonical members X,M_1,…,M_{n−1} have sizes at least n,max(r,n−1),…,max(r,1). Every member other than these and ∅ has size at least r. Since r<n for n>1, summation gives T≥n(n+1)/2+r(r−1)/2+r(m−n−1). The n=1 case also satisfies the displayed formula directly.
claims.search_method: Exact incidence double counting and closed-form evaluation of the canonical-size sum.

claims.claim: Frankl’s conjecture holds whenever the smallest positive member of the reduced family has size r≥n/2. In particular, it holds for every family with at most six inequivalent active elements.
claims.evidence: For the preceding L, exact expansion gives 2L−nm=(2r−n)(m−n−1)+r(r−1). Both terms are nonnegative when r≥n/2, since m≥n+1, so the average frequency is at least m/2. A reduced counterexample would have r≥3 by the singleton and two-set results but r<n/2 by this result, forcing n≥7. The checker confirms the integer identity over a broad parameter grid; the displayed symbolic expansion proves it generally.
claims.search_method: Symbolic integer algebra plus an exact-arithmetic checker.

claims.claim: A normalized separating counterexample with parameters n,m,r must have odd m and satisfy an explicit quantitative lower bound.
claims.evidence: Take the normalized representative supplied by the empty-set, odd-cardinality, and incidence-quotient reductions. Odd m gives d_x≤(m−1)/2 and hence T≤n(m−1)/2. Combining this with the incidence lower bound yields (n−2r)m≥n(n+2−2r)+r²−3r. Since a counterexample has r<n/2, division is valid. Also d_max≥n and d_max≤(m−1)/2 give m≥2n+1, proving the stated maximum of the two lower bounds.
claims.search_method: Direct combination of the normalization lemmas and exact symbolic rearrangement; integer specializations were checker-tested.

claims.claim: Any normalized separating counterexample on seven elements must have at least 25 members.
claims.evidence: Here r=3 and odd m≥21. At m=21 the lower and upper incidence totals are both 70; equality makes all frequencies 10 and forces M_2={x_3,…,x_7}. Any set containing x_1 but not x_2 would union with M_2 to the unavailable X\{x_2}; equal frequencies then contradict separation. At m=23 the totals satisfy 76≤T≤77. If |M_2|=5, separation forces d_1<d_2, whence T=76 and d=(10,11,…,11), but only X and five triples containing {x_1,x_2} can contain x_1. If M_2=X\{x_2}, all slack is consumed; closure uniquely forces M_5={x_4,x_6,x_7} and M_6={x_4,x_5,x_7}. Exhaustion of all 7-bit triples leaves only 10 possible further triples although 15 are required. The checker reproduces all bounds and residual counts exactly.
claims.search_method: Complete proof split for m=21 and m=23, with exhaustive exact-bitmask checking of every residual subset case.

claims.claim: Frankl’s bound holds if the family is closed under both unions and intersections.
claims.evidence: After adjoining ∅ if needed, choose an inclusion-minimal nonempty A. For x∈A and U avoiding x, U∩A is a proper family member contained in A, so minimality forces U∩A=∅. The map U↦U∪A is therefore an injection from members avoiding x to members containing x, recoverable by deleting A. This proves the augmented bound, which is at least the original threshold.
claims.search_method: Direct minimal-member injection proof, including the case where ∅ must first be adjoined.

claims.claim: Exact enumeration verifies Frankl’s conjecture for every labelled ground set of size at most five and verifies the tight-clean power-set conclusion there.
claims.evidence: The exact bitmask DFS generated 4, 14, 122, 4,960, and 2,771,104 union-closed families for n=1,…,5. It found zero Frankl counterexamples and zero non-power-set families containing ∅ with nonzero distinct columns and every frequency at most half. Ordering subsets by nonincreasing size makes every new union obligation already decided, proving completeness and uniqueness of the enumeration. Independent enumeration of every assignment agreed through n=4. The n=0 case is trivial.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive integer-bitmask DFS over every labelled family, independently cross-checked by all-assignment enumeration through n=4.

claims.claim: The natural strengthening “every smallest nonempty member contains a Frankl element” is false.
claims.evidence: Exact checking found 19 distinct members, all 361 ordered unions present, minimum positive size 3, and frequencies (9,9,9,14,14,14,17). Thus the minimum member {1,2,3} contains no element occurring in at least 19/2 members, while the family itself still has Frankl elements.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive exact-integer verification of distinctness, union closure, sizes, and frequencies for the displayed witness.

target_evidence: The exact target requires either a proof of Frankl’s conjecture for every finite union-closed family or a genuine counterexample. The draft expressly provides neither: it proves reductions, several subclasses, bounded enumeration, and constraints on a hypothetical counterexample; its 19-set example refutes only a stronger auxiliary statement and itself satisfies Frankl’s bound. Those are correct and material but incomplete, so VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS is appropriate. The final writeup explicitly disclaims a complete resolution, and claimed_resolution is PARTIAL, making that resolution claim ACCURATE.
